verdicts.reason: Proposing measurable indicators and reporting triggers is a separate axis from analyzing failure conditions and safeguards; a comment can do either without the other.
Spotting a category the rule wrongly conflates does not require any cross-reference to another identified rule or docket.
X requires load-bearing quantities (which may come from the commenter's own operations), while Y requires a locatable external source and can be satisfied with no numbers at all.
A precise proposed threshold or replacement wording can be offered without ever naming the exact provision it targets, which is the requirement Y turns on.
Both score a traced step-by-step chain from the requirement to concrete effects, with the identical zero anchor of bare assertion of help or harm.
Rebutting an objection to one's own position is distinct from supplying a substitute approach; a comment can rebut without proposing anything.
Engaging the proposal's own provisions is not the same as invoking and applying governing statutory or precedential language.
X scores how the proposal as written could be executed; Y scores whether a different design is offered, and a supportive comment can be high on X with no alternative at all.
Designing forward-looking tracking and verification is distinct from quantifying effects against a baseline.
Weighing competing objectives and justifying a balance is distinct from supplying a concrete substitute for the provision opposed.
Correcting an error or ambiguity in the agency's wording is different from the precision of the change requested; a precise threshold can be proposed without any textual correction.
Both score whether legal claims are grounded in identified statutory, regulatory, or precedential language applied to the proposal, with the same zero anchor of unsupported legal conclusions.
A single causal chain to a direct consequence is not the same as tracing effects across connected systems, actors, or jurisdictions.
Y credits acknowledging and answering any specific objection or trade-off, while X demands the strongest opposing rationale stated accurately and answered on its own terms.
Unequal incidence of costs and benefits across groups is a distributional claim; edge-case coverage is about contexts where the mechanism operates differently, which need not involve equity.
A developed ultra-vires argument and the mere presence of part/section CFR citations are independent; either can occur without the other.
Pinpointing a proposed provision and requesting a revision does not require identifying or applying governing legal language.
Y scores the separation of what is accepted from what is disputed; a comment can pinpoint a provision and demand a revision with no calibrated partial agreement at all.
X specifically requires two competing readings of a term with divergent consequences, while Y also credits correcting a factual error or misstatement in the proposal's text.
Supplying rule-specific numeric figures is not the same as specifying an exact actionable change; evidence-heavy comments often request nothing concrete.
X is steelmanning and answering the best contrary rationale; Y additionally requires explicit comparison of competing objectives and a justified balance.
Proposing an implementable alternative design and proposing measurement or verification machinery are unrelated contributions.
Offering a workable substitute design is distinct from explicitly weighing competing objectives and justifying a balance.
Both score firsthand situated observation translated into a rule-relevant generalizable implication, with the same zero anchor of unanalyzed anecdote.
A conflation internal to this rule's categories is different from conflicts, duplication, or coordination needs across other rules and agencies.
Locating a provision and asking for a revision is orthogonal to demonstrating statutory authority or interpretive fit.
An internal conflation of sub-cases requires no other named legal instrument, which is exactly what Y demands.
Laying out a causal and behavioral-response chain is independent of acknowledging and answering opposing considerations.
Pinpointing a provision and requesting a revision does not entail identifying sub-cases the rule wrongly treats alike.
X scores what the proposal fails to say or commit to; Y scores engagement with a provision that exists plus a concrete revision to it.
X centers on failure conditions and safeguards; Y centers on heterogeneity of contexts and populations, and a comment on rural-versus-urban operation can be high on Y with no failure analysis.
An unaddressed scenario inside this rule's text can be raised with no comparison to any other identified rule or docket.
Proposing a substitute approach is distinct from accurately stating and answering the strongest opposing rationale.
Y requires identifying an error, ambiguity, or misstatement in the quoted wording; X only requires locating a provision and requesting a concrete revision.
Both score explicit separation of established fact from assumption and inference with calibrated confidence, sharing the zero anchor of presenting contested claims as certain.
Both score whether the requested change is stated as concrete replacement language, thresholds, or defined procedures rather than a vague directional ask, with identical zero anchors.
Correcting the operative rule text is different from engaging the preamble's rationale, impact figures, and cited studies; comments commonly do one and not the other.
Answering an objection to one's own position is not the same as explicitly weighing competing benefits, costs, and affected parties.
Rule-specific numeric figures and comparison against another identified rule or docket are independent contributions.
X requires a concrete unaddressed scenario in the rule text, while Y also credits unassigned responsibilities and undelivered commitments that involve no scenario at all.
Pinpointing a provision of this rule is orthogonal to identifying conflicts or duplication across related rules, agencies, and workflows.
Both score whether the commenter supplies its own monetary estimate of compliance cost with a stated basis, with the same zero anchor of no figures.
Supplying rule-specific numbers and naming the exact provision plus a concrete revision are separable; quantitative comments often request nothing specific.
Correcting the wording of this proposal requires no comparison against another identified rule, docket, or precedent.
Both score whether the comment proposes concrete measurement, monitoring, or validation procedures tied to a decision, and both penalize vague calls for more study or oversight.
Both require naming a particular other legal instrument and reasoning explicitly about its consistency with the proposal, with the same zero anchor of treating the rule in isolation.
Both score whether an implementable substitute that still serves the agency's underlying objective is offered rather than bare rejection, with the same zero anchor.
Y requires a named place, facility, or institution, while X is satisfied by any identified group plus an exposure mechanism, so a firm-size analysis scores high on X and low on Y.
Y additionally requires that the named instance cut against a premise the agency's action depends on; a real precedent cited to support one's own claim scores high on X and low on Y.
Cross-system spillovers and long-horizon or cumulative time-path effects are separate dimensions of consequence.
Rule-specific numbers and application of governing legal text are unrelated criteria.
Both score explicit comparison and weighing of competing benefits, costs, and objections, with the same zero anchor of one-sided advocacy.
Handling tradeoffs is unrelated to focus and prioritization of recommendations; a diffuse comment can still weigh tradeoffs well.
Y credits any specific objection answered with reasoning, while X requires explicit comparison of competing objectives and a justification of the recommended balance.
Rebutting an external objection is the opposite posture from conceding a genuine limitation of one's own position; a comment can rebut and never concede.
Near-verbatim restatements: both score identifiable studies, records, or data relevant to the proposal against a zero anchor of unsupported assertion.
Correcting the agency's wording and supplying rule-specific numeric figures are independent contributions.
Both score concrete execution detail about who must act and with what systems or workflows, sharing the zero anchor of demanding a result with no engagement with execution.
Firsthand operational description and emotional intensity are unrelated and often inversely present.
Y requires a concrete scenario the rule text leaves unresolved, while X requires naming a provision and requesting a revision; either can occur alone.
An unaddressed scenario is a gap in coverage, while a conflated distinction is over-broad uniform treatment of cases the rule does cover.
Both score whether a specific, implementable substitute is offered instead of bare objection, with the same zero anchor of support or opposition with nothing proposed.
An error in what the proposal says and an omission of what it fails to say are different targets; gap analysis need not quote any wording.
Both score an explicit step-by-step chain through behavior or implementation to a specific consequence, with the same zero anchor of asserted harm or benefit.
Both score whether an alternative is specified concretely enough to implement, with the same zero anchor of bare approval, rejection, or an unelaborated demand.
Proposing measurement and verification machinery is unrelated to naming a provision and requesting a revision.
Both score operational detail about responsible actors, workflows, and system dependencies that determine whether the rule can be executed, with the same zero anchor.

Both score reasoning about consistency with the surrounding regulatory system against the same zero anchor of treating the proposal in isolation, though Y is broader in also crediting workflow coordination.
Quantifying an effect against a baseline is independent of tracing second-order effects across connected systems.
The precision of the requested change can be high while the comment never anchors it to an identified proposed provision, which is what Y requires.
X is a scenario the text does not reach, while Y is an error or misstatement in language the text does contain; the targets differ.
Both score identification of which specific groups bear which costs or benefits plus the concrete exposure mechanism, with the same zero anchor of generic appeals to the public.
Engaging multiple provisions and explaining their operation is independent of supplying rule-specific numeric figures.
Cross-rule consistency and design of monitoring or verification are unrelated criteria.

Both score whether the comment names responsible actors, required systems and resources, and the practical conditions for the rule to work, with the same zero anchor of treating implementation as automatic.
Both score an explicit step-by-step mechanism from the requirement to concrete effects, with the same zero anchor of bare assertion of consequence.
Both score whether a concrete alternative regulatory design is described specifically enough to be adopted, with the same zero anchor of proposing nothing.
X rewards explaining how multiple provisions operate even with no edit requested, while Y requires a concrete revision to a pinpointed provision.
Explaining how provisions operate is not the same as identifying a specific error, ambiguity, or misstatement in the quoted wording and giving the correct reading.
